extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory and constitutional government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical standards for assessing the usefulness, dangers, and duties of a constitutional sovereign and the social/political role of the House of Lords. The page sets out when a monarch or an aristocratic chamber is beneficial or harmful and explains necessary political conditions for stable Cabinet government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity/coherence of parliamentary majorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cabinet polity requires a parliament that can choose a sufficiently permanent executive; when three parties exist with rapidly oscillating preferences, the primary condition of Cabinet government is not satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by 1858 events: a numerically weakest party may cast deciding votes but forfeits support for its own candidate, producing unstable, revocable choices. Prolonged, exaggerated oscillation between parties makes a reliable ministry impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate cross-party cooperation to sustain government
rubrics_metrics.description: The moderate people of every party must combine to support the government which, on the whole, suits every party best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination produces stable administrations (example: Lord Palmerston's administration maintained by moderate Conservatives and Radicals); without such moderation, there is no fixity in the choosers and governments will be unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's discernment/selective power in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign with a genius for discernment can assist by selecting and, if possible, maintaining the statesman whom the moderate party would ultimately accept, thus aiding equilibrium in shifting party configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The monarch may have opportunities to try different combinations (call on 'A B' or 'X Y'); discreet exercise of this selection can be of 'incalculable value' during complex party divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of limited ability in hereditary sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory and experience suggest a constitutional sovereign will generally be a man of but common or inferior ability due to poor princely education and hereditary decline in faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume perpetual inheritance of exceptional discretion; an exquisite discretion is at least as rare as genius and unlikely to be continuously entailed in a dynasty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's wisdom often best shown by well-considered inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional king's greatest wisdom will often be in refraining from interposing his own selection or action, thereby allowing Parliament to assume responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Queen and Prince Albert (1857–1859) refrained from obtruding choices; overuse of royal agency can delay beneficial crystallisation of intrinsic parliamentary forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's proper constitutional role: consult, encourage, warn
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a constitutional monarchy the sovereign has three rights—the right to be consulted, the right to encourage, the right to warn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rights should be used without usurping responsibility: give counsel, provide memoranda, indicate objections ('I WARN'), and support ministers once they act, but avoid arbitrary interference or later modification of measures to which royal sanction was given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private audiences impair free argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences between a minister and his sovereign cannot be conferences of pure argument; the monarch's presence induces deference so ministers cannot argue as freely or incisively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited example: Lord Chatham (who was 'intoxicated' by access to the king) — physical posture and reverence diminish a minister's capacity to refute the sovereign's bad arguments or present his best ones; thus royal private influence skews debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution prerogative is a potent political lever
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign's legal power to dissolve Parliament (or threaten to) can be used as a tacit political threat to influence ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: George III used the shadow of a possible successor to make ministers tremble; such a power can help a sovereign back a view by making the possibility of a new Parliament implicit leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of monarch's institutional memory and accumulated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A long-reigning, sagacious king acquires experience and consecutive knowledge of complex transactions that few ministers can match, enabling him to recall precedent events and advise effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The king can act like a permanent under-secretary, reminding ministers of past errors or instructive examples and providing memoranda that suggest materials for consideration; this cumulative influence can root out impracticable plans and promote better ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession cannot reliably produce a line of wise monarchs
rubrics_metrics.description: History shows constitutional royalty rarely endures beyond the generation that founded it; one cannot expect a continuous succession of useful limited monarchs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the first two Georges were ignorant of English affairs; continental founders (Louis Philippe, Victor Emmanuel, Leopold) are exceptions; reliance on heredity for consistent excellence is misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only certain princes are fit material for constitutional kingship
rubrics_metrics.description: The only fit material for a constitutional king is a prince who begins early to reign, is superior to pleasure, willing to labour in youth, and has a natural genius for discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idle, pleasure-loving prince is unlikely to acquire the habit of business; when accession occurs late in life the chance of effective labor is smaller. Therefore, the suitability of the monarch depends on early personal disposition and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: A meddling or insane monarch is exceptionally harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: An active, meddling, or half-insane king can be one of the worst forms of government, exercising secret, obstinate, and often wrong influence that overpowers ministers and produces irreparable evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: George III is cited as prolonging wars and obstructing wise plans; the evils of a bad monarch can outlive him and be hard to detect or prevent because they are 'inscrutable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid instituting a 'grand elector' or governor-for-life
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a governor-for-life (an appointed chooser of ministers) is a voluntary erection of an artificial encumbrance that becomes inevitably partisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an office would be contested by parties, filled at their pleasure, and likely to be used as an auxiliary by the strongest party; colonies do not need such an office to launch administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court influences (favourites, mistresses) corrupt governance especially when parties are divided
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a Court there can be evil influence from favourites and intimates, which is particularly dangerous when Parliament is perplexed and parties divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Walpole relying on the king's mistress; influence of the Marchioness of Conyngham; several Italian changes of government attributed to court intrigues. These sinister agencies are most effective when other forces are troubled.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords as a symbol that imposes reverence and suggests mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of nobility imposes on the common people a symbol of mind and awakens a sensation of obedience that a common clever man would not obtain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even an insolvent old squire commands respect the newly-rich lack; the Lords' symbolic authority helps awaken deference among the 'coarse, dull, contracted multitude' and serves a useful social function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as counterbalance to the worship of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary nobility prevents the unqualified rule of wealth and acts as a check on the 'religion of gold' by preserving an alternative social ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having two idols (rank and wealth) allows competition between idolatries so that 'the true worship gets a chance'; England's aristocracy keeps mere wealth from buying full social acceptance ('no country where a "poor devil of a millionaire is so ill off as in England"').

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy preserves manner/style (social grace) as a public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary rank tends to transmit manner and style—an unconscious social art—that is valuable in society and often concentrated among the aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style in daily intercourse is likened to the art of literary expression; reverence for inherited nobility often rests on the probable possession of a 'faculty' for refined social manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy prevents office-idolatry and the undue exaltation of minor officials
rubrics_metrics.description: An order of nobility helps prevent the rule or idolisation of petty office and the exaggerated social prestige of minor public functionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts drawn with continental France where subordinate employees are over-admired; in England the social prestige instead tends to attach to important public offices that require mind, which is judged socially beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public offices requiring intellect should confer social prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Good social organisation awards prestige to major public offices that genuinely require mind, thereby preserving a healthy social reward structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an Under-Secretary of State (2000 pounds a year) commands more social standing than a director of a finance company (5000 pounds), which the essay regards as a social advantage that limits the dominion of wealth alone.
